questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=2y-xy,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2-x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )+(2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x+y},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{1}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $h(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂h}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$

questions.problem: Given that $h(x,y,z)=xyz,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂h}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂h}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=yz,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}=xz\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =rz\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta } & =-(rz\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}z{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}z({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={r}^{2}z\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{3}+{z}^{4},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂r},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =3{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(3{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +3{r}^{2}{sin}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2xyz\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2{r}^{2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

                    Calculating the Derivative of a Cartesian Function With Respect to Plane Polar Coordinates
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\dfrac12x^2+y^2,$ find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta,$ where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating the Derivative of a Polar Function With Respect to Cartesian Coordinates
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $w(r, \theta)=r \cos 3\theta,$ find $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}\cos\theta - \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta}\sin\theta
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta +3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $w(x,y,z)=z^3(x^2+2y^2),$ find $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\cos\theta, y=r\sin\theta,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂w}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=2x{z}^{3},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=4y{z}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =2r{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =4r{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =-(2r{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(4r{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-2{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Given a function $f(x,y),$ how do we calculate the partial derivatives $f_r$ and $f_\theta,$ where $(r,\theta)$ are plane polar coordinates?

To do this, we can use the multivariable chain rule. First, let's write down our tree diagram.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14156360/assets/7f19c4a682b30f1eea1d9c1be7da83bd77ba137173f25eb9c7e5cf253abba015.png)

From the tree diagram, we can see that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's take the partial derivatives of $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂r} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  &  &  & \frac{∂y}{∂r} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂x}{∂\theta } & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  &  &  & \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these results into the multivariable chain rule, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

To do this, we can use the multivariable chain rule. First, let's write down our tree diagram.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14156360/assets/7f19c4a682b30f1eea1d9c1be7da83bd77ba137173f25eb9c7e5cf253abba015.png)

From the tree diagram, we can see that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's take the partial derivatives of $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂r} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  &  &  & \frac{∂y}{∂r} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂x}{∂\theta } & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  &  &  & \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these results into the multivariable chain rule, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Differentiating of a Function Given in Polar Coordinates With Respect to Cartesian Coordinates
tutorials.problem:
Up to now, we've been using the following formulas:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{r} & ={f}_{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {f}_{\theta } & =-r{f}_{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We can treat the above as a system of equations in the "unknowns" $f_x$ and $f_y.$ Solving this system gives explicit expressions for $f_x$ and $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\theta.$

For example, suppose we want an explicit formula for $f_x.$ We can eliminate $f_y$ by multiplying the first equation by $r\cos\theta$ and the second equation by $\sin\theta$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}r{f}_{r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =r{f}_{x}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ {f}_{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-r{f}_{x}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first gives

$$
r f_r \cos\theta - f_\theta \sin\theta = r f_x(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta),
$$

which simplifies to

$$
f_x = f_r \cos\theta - \dfrac1r f_\theta \sin\theta.
$$

We can use a similar procedure to write $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\theta.$ Our results as summarized below:

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \cos \theta
						-\dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\sin \theta\[1ex]
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \sin \theta
						+ \dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\cos \theta
}
$$

tutorials.name: The Multivariable Chain Rule With Cylindrical Polar Coordinates
tutorials.problem:
Given a function of three variables $f(x,y,z),$ we can find formulas for $f_r, f_\theta,$ and $f_z,$ where $(r,\theta,z)$ are cylindrical polar coordinates. The results that we need are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the first and second equations are identical to the equations derived for plane polar coordinates, as we would expect. 

The difference here is that we now have a third equation that deals with the $z$-dependence. But since the $z$-coordinate is the same in both Cartesian and cylindrical polar coordinates, we can simply differentiate with respect to $z$ as usual.

Let's see an example.

tutorials.name: The Multivariable Chain Rule With Spherical Polar Coordinates
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that we have a function $f(x,y,z),$ and we wish to find formulas for $f_\rho,$ $f_\theta,$ and $f_\phi$, where $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ are spherical polar coordinates.

Using the multivariable chain rule, it can be shown that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\rho } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂ϕ} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\frac{∂f}{∂z}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

You might want to try deriving these formulas for yourself!
tutorials.title: The Multivariable Chain Rule With Spherical Polar Coordinates
tutorials.content:
Suppose that we have a function $f(x,y,z),$ and we wish to find formulas for $f_\rho,$ $f_\theta,$ and $f_\phi$, where $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ are spherical polar coordinates.

Using the multivariable chain rule, it can be shown that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\rho } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂ϕ} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\frac{∂f}{∂z}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

You might want to try deriving these formulas for yourself!
